prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a specific invention with a clear before-and-after. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating many atoms at once, and Ye's group took the concept to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and to many-body-enhanced operation. From the atomic-structure side, the magic-wavelength condition, blackbody and lattice-light shifts and the systematic budget are well understood and have been reproduced independently in Sr, Yb and Hg laboratories worldwide. The impact is concrete and lasting: the planned redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and tests of fundamental physics. It has by far the broadest opening support of any shortlisted entry (all eight members ranked it, four in their top three, three first places), and the two-person configuration is clean and defensible. I do not equate that support with merit, but my own assessment independently agrees.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is partial prior recognition of adjacent ground: the 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch) for frequency-comb spectroscopy and the 2012 prize (Wineland) for control of single trapped ions. A committee could view the lattice clock as a refinement of already honoured technology, and could also fairly ask whether other lattice-clock contributors (Ytterbium work, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, Tokyo) or the early lattice-clock proposals are being underweighted by a two-name credit. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so one could also argue for waiting. I judge the lattice clock a distinct invention rather than an extension, but this is the point on which the case is most contestable.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the clock only fourth and notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes already covered adjacent ground, so the area may be considered partially recognised, while placing topological insulators first.
responses.response: I take the overlap concern seriously, but I read it differently. Hall and Hansch gave the frequency measurement tool and Wineland the control of single quantum systems; neither includes trapping thousands of neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that Doppler, recoil and lattice shifts cancel, which is what moved accuracy from 1e-16 to 1e-18. That is a new invention, not a refinement. I also respect the case for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, but I find its attribution weaker: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation and the three-dimensional work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others) lies outside the credited names, and the 2016 prize already covered topological phases. The clock has no comparable allocation hole.

responses.point: Olsson ranks spherical-aberration correction first as a clear invention with a concrete before-and-after, and values its broad impact in materials science, while placing the clock second.
responses.response: I agree that the corrector is a real invention, and I rank it third for that reason. Rose, Haider and Urban have a natural three-way split and the recognition is mature. My reservations are two. First, the credit is contested by the independent STEM-corrector development (Krivanek and collaborators), as you and Pearce both note, and a three-name prize would have to exclude them. Second, its impact is as an enabling tool for materials characterisation, whereas the lattice clock changes a fundamental measurement standard and opens tests of physics itself. Both fit the invention criterion, but I put the clock ahead; I would gladly see the corrector as the next candidate if the committee prefers an instrumentation theme.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the clock first as the decisive improvement in what can be measured, with Katori and Ye the natural pair, and flags the wider comb and stable-laser ecosystem and a connection to Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree with the pairing and the maturity assessment, and I appreciate the disclosed connection to Hall's laboratory, which should be handled as a recusal question for Ye's case. I would qualify one point: the comb and ultrastable-laser technology is a real input to the clock's performance, but it is already recognised in 2005, and I do not think that argues for adding names. I would keep the citation to the lattice clock itself, and not broaden it to timekeeping in general, so that it stays clearly distinct from the earlier prizes.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the clock first as a clean instrument-driven advance and places IceCube second, noting that credit among IceCube, AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers is unresolved.
responses.response: I share the view of the clock as an instrument-driven advance with broad downstream use. On IceCube I am an outsider, but your own attribution caveat seems decisive for me: a Halzen and Karle prize leaves open the claims of the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND pioneers, and source identification (TXS 0506+056 at about 3 sigma, NGC 1068 at about 4 sigma) is still maturing. By contrast the clock is confirmed at the 1e-18 level in many laboratories. I would be interested to hear whether you think the neutrino case can be made more definite before this cycle ends.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
How to weigh Katori's early lattice proposal and first demonstration against Ye's accuracy and many-body work, and whether other lattice-clock contributors have a competing claim.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes this the right year or a later one.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. My documented collaborations (Anne L'Huillier, the Lund and ETH Zurich attosecond groups, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) concern attosecond photoionisation and highly charged ions, not the lattice clock, and I have no documented tie to the other shortlisted candidates. I note that I am a theoretical atomic physicist and judge the atomic-structure side of the clock better than the experimental engineering.
